 Obama teases Trump about reaction to Cheesecake Factory comment 
 2:05
 Former President Barack Obama said President Donald Trump’s administration “mobilized” a “government response” to “that joke” he made comparing White House decor to that of the Cheesecake Factory.
 “That was the interesting thing about how the administration responded to the speech I gave the other day: They did not dispute what I said about them being directly responsible for rising prices. They did not argue with that,” Obama said tonight at a rally in Georgia. “They did not deny terrorists were contributing to higher costs for families. They didn’t say anything about that. But he was very upset about the Cheesecake Factory comment. He took great umbrage.”
 Over the weekend, Obama criticized the gilded decor changes Trump has made to the White House since his return to office.
 “There’s gold everywhere,” Obama told Democrats at a rally in Cleveland on Saturday. “What’s up with the gold? Everything — more gold!”
 He continued: “He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory .”
 The clip quickly blanketed the internet, and Trump on Monday defended both his love for renovation projects and his design style.
 Tonight, Obama doubled down, saying the Cheesecake Factory and other restaurants were “his jam for about a decade.”
 “I am the father of two daughters. Do you think I could have survived their childhood without going to the Cheesecake Factory? I lived at Chuck E. Cheese and California Pizza Kitchen and the Cheesecake Factory,” Obama quipped.
 “The real problem is that prices have gotten so high, a lot of folks can barely afford to go out to eat,” he added. “You would think that this administration would be spending time worrying about that.”
 CNN’s David Mack contributed reporting.

 Trump says he'll "consider" putting Space Academy in Ohio if Husted wins
 By Alejandra Jaramillo 
 US President Donald Trump shakes hands with US Senator Jon Husted, Republican from Ohio, during a midterm campaign rally at Shoemaker Center in Chillicothe, Ohio on October 28. 
 Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty Images 
 President Donald Trump told Ohio voters that he would consider putting the new US Space Academy in their state if Republican incumbent Sen. Jon Husted wins next week.
 “And I wanted you to know that if Jon Husted wins, I am going to consider putting the Space Academy right here,” Trump told the crowd at his rally in Chillicothe, Ohio, six days before the midterm elections.
 “If you win,” he added. “And everybody wants it. Every state, they all want it.”
 Ohio formally submitted its bid to host the academy ahead of NASA’s deadline earlier this week. Several states have applied to host the campus.
 Ohio leaders — including GOP Sen. Bernie Moreno, who joined Trump at Wednesday’s rally — have proposed an initial $300 million investment to bring it to the state.
 Trump signed an executive order earlier this year establishing a “United States Space Academy,” designed to offer the same kind of tuition-free, four-year degree as US military academies like West Point.

 Watch: CNN's Manu Raju presses Ashley Hinson on her vote on Trump's war powers 
 0:38
 Republican congresswoman Ashley Hinson, who is locked in one of the most competitive Senate contests this cycle for a seat in Iowa, showed limited interest in answering questions today as CNN pressed her about her stance on the Iran war and a recent shift in her public messaging.
 CNN’s Manu Raju caught up with Hinson after a campaign event in Bancroft, Iowa, a two hour drive from Des Moines. As she walked briskly to her campaign bus, Raju asked her about her shifting the campaign’s message away from asserting herself as Trump’s “strongest ally in the Senate” — as she did last year – as well as her votes against limiting President Donald Trump’s powers in Iran, despite having called herself for an end to the war.
 Hinson told Raju she’s “always been bipartisan” when asked about her efforts to emphasize bipartisanship rather than her close alliance with Trump. “I had 1,700 bipartisan votes and my first two bills signed into law were signed under Biden. So I’m going to work with anybody to get things done for Iowa.”
 When asked to square her votes opposing measures that would limit Trump’s war powers in Iran with her public declarations about wanting to see an end to the conflict, she said, “We don’t need another resolution. We need our US military and the president to end the war, and that’s what I feel.”
 She ignored further questions as she boarded her campaign bus, flanked by a team of aides and security.

 "Georgia will bow to no king," Sen. Jon Ossoff says at rally with Obama
 By Jeff Zeleny and Taylor Romine 
 Sen. Jon Ossoff, who is running for reelection in Georgia, accused the Trump administration of corruption, telling supporters at a rally, “Georgia will bow to no king.”
 “In six days, Georgia will rebuke the crook President Donald Trump with such clarity and power that no president will dare such abuses again for centuries,” Ossoff said at the Atlanta event before former President Barack Obama took the stage.
 Ossoff, the Democratic incumbent who once was seen as the biggest Republican target of the midterm elections, implored Georgia voters to send a message to Trump in next week’s election.
 He also reiterated his criticism of Trump on issues like affordability, immigration, and the Iran war.
 “A wave is building,” Ossoff said, “The kind of wave that comes once a generation when the people have been pushed too far and decide that enough is enough.”

 Trump asks why Acton's mother's statements in Ramaswamy ad are his problem
 By Betsy Klein in Chillicothe, Ohio
 President Donald Trump speaks during a campaign rally at the Shoemaker Center at Ohio University Chillicothe in Chillicothe, Ohio, on October 28. 
 Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images 
 President Donald Trump doubled down on a controversial ad from Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy featuring his Democratic opponent Amy Acton’s estranged mother, telling a crowd in the Buckeye State Wednesday that any pushback is “very unfair.”
 The ad has been widely condemned on both sides of the aisle, including by Ohio’s Republican Gov. Mike DeWine.
 Acton’s mother calls her daughter a “liar” in the ad. Acton has said she hasn’t seen her mother since she was 12 years old, when her mother lost custody of her children as Acton’s stepfather was indicted by a grand jury on charges of sexually abusing her.
 With Ramaswamy sitting on the sidelines of the rally, Trump questioned what would have happened if his own mother had called him a liar (some of Trump’s family members have spoken out against him in the past).
 “I would say the press would be getting Pulitzer prizes if they reported it. But with Vivek, how dare he put that information?” Trump said, not mentioning that Acton’s situation involved child sexual abuse.
 He continued, “The mother said that Amy Acton, the daughter, is a liar. That she’s no good. That she lied about the opponent. How the hell is that his problem? Very unfair,” prompting loud applause from the gymnasium crowd.
 Trump claimed that if Ramaswamy were a Democrat, there would not have been criticism.
 “Believe me, it’s a very unfair situation,” he said.

 Trump: Obama campaigning for Democrats is "good" because he backed Harris and "lost"
 By Betsy Klein in Chillicothe, Ohio
 President Donald Trump downplayed concerns about former President Barack Obama hitting the campaign trail ahead of Tuesday’s consequential midterm elections, saying Obama supported both Hillary Clinton and Kamala Harris and “he lost.”
 “I took heat because Obama, who is, I mean, I always worry when he campaigns against me because he got involved with Hillary Clinton. He was really — oh, and then he lost,” Trump said in Chillicothe at the same time Obama rallied in Georgia.
 He continued: “He then got involved with Kamala, and he lost. And he lost.”
 Trump said he was told Obama was coming out on the campaign trail. His reaction: “I said, ’That’s good.’”
 The president alluded to recent comments from Obama attacking his aesthetic changes to the White House, defending his preoccupation with projects like his massive ballroom, among others.
 “The White House, I think, is the number one symbol of our country, and we can’t have a White House with broken windows, with broken stone that hasn’t been painted in 30 years,” Trump said.

 Democratic gubernatorial candidate ties Republican opponent to Trump at metro Atlanta rally
 By Isa Mudannayake 
 Georgia gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms speaks at The Arena at Southlake in Morrow, Georgia, on Wednesday, October 28. 
 Will Lanzoni/CNN 
 Democratic gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms repeatedly tied Republican opponent Rick Jackson to President Donald Trump during a Wednesday rally in metro Atlanta.
 Bottoms, who repeatedly referred to Jackson as “Slick Rick,” said Jackson is “running to be Donald Trump’s favorite governor.”
 “His number one priority will be to do whatever his big daddy Donald Trump tells him to do,” she said.
 A former Atlanta mayor, Bottoms would be the nation’s first Black female governor if elected, as several Black candidates vie for gubernatorial seats in eight states.
 Surrounded by supporters chanting “no Slick Rick,” Bottoms emphasized raising teacher salaries, increasing healthcare and building more affordable housing, which she said contrasts with Jackson’s goal of continuing to get “rich off the backs of taxpayers.”
 President Barack Obama was also slated to speak at the event after US Sen. Jon Ossoff, who is running for reelection.

 Trump grouses about coverage of remarks on Husted's body: “It didn’t look good for me.”
 By Donald Judd 
 President Donald Trump spent his opening remarks at his Wednesday rally in Chillicothe, Ohio reflecting on the physical attributes of Sen. Jon Husted, grousing over media coverage of his comments from the trail as he again spoke admiringly of the incumbent Republican.
 “I was examining that man for his physical prowess, and I got it — when he stood up, I looked at him, I looked him all over the place, and I should have never said what I said, but I said I started by looking at his ass, and it was strong as hell,” Trump said. “And the problem is the fake news … they said, ‘I looked at his ass,’ and they cut. And then they, all night long, they say, ‘Why did he say that?’ In other words, they just went cut, and it didn’t look good for me.”
 Trump has seemed preoccupied with Husted’s physical appearance since campaigning for the Ohio senator during a rally in Ohio earlier this month. During that rally, he told supporters he hadn’t noticed Husted’s appearance until former NFL Coach Jon Gruden told him Husted played football in college.
 “He was an All-American football player, and when Jon Gruden said he was the best player on the team — and I think they were, like, a championship team, a great team,” the president said. “And I don’t do this with men very often. I started examining his body, because I didn’t know he was a great athlete.”
 Since then, he’s brought up Husted’s physical appearance at campaign rallies across the country, including stops in North Carolina, Michigan and Texas, where he joked he’d say the same thing about Republican candidate Ken Paxton, “but I’m not sure your body is going to qualify.”

 Trump defends himself against anti-Epstein protestors
 By Alejandra Jaramillo 
 President Donald Trump speaks on stage during a campaign rally at the Shoemaker Center at Ohio University on October 28, 2026 in Chillicothe, Ohio. President Trump is rallying support for Republican candidates in Ohio ahead of the midterm elections. 
 Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images 
 President Donald Trump on Wednesday bristled at hecklers who interrupted him minutes into his rally in Chillicothe, Ohio, breaking from his usual habit of laughing off protesters and instead defending how he handled his relationship with Jeffrey Epstein.
 “So that guy, he’s right out of the radical left playbook,” Trump told the crowd at the Shoemaker Center in Chillicothe, after a protestor was forced out. “This guy was very nondescript, but I will say this: you know, he mentioned Epstein.”
 Visibly irritated, the president went on to say he had kicked the deceased convicted sex offender out of his Palm Beach club years ago.
 “I threw Jeffrey Epstein the hell out of Mar-a-Lago,” Trump said, adding, “That was a great thing I did.”
 He sought to tie Epstein to Democrats, saying, “He was a Democrat,” and claimed he himself had been “totally exonerated.” He also claimed they were “professional protestors. They get money.”
 The smaller venue made the disruptions harder to ignore than at some of Trump’s larger events, though he’s faced a growing number of protesters at his midterm rallies in recent weeks. He usually jokingly brushes them off, telling crowds his rallies “are something” and that protesters will be “going back home to mom,” and sometimes even commenting on their physique.

 Political tricks in 2026 and the time JFK ran against two Joe Russos
 Analysis by Zachary B. Wolf 
 From today’s What Matters newsletter ( sign up here ): 
 It’s a footnote in the archives of the JFK Presidential Library.
 John F. Kennedy won his crowded first congressional primary in Boston against two men named Joe Russo. According to the politician Russo, “They put in this other Joseph Russo in order to complicate the names.”
 Consider that trivia as Republicans seize on The Times’ report that Democrats schemed to put a second Dan Sullivan on Alaska’s ranked-choice ballot for US Senate and dilute support for incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan.
 Dirty tricks are nothing new. Watergate began as an effort — an illegal effort — by President Richard Nixon to get a leg up on Democrats.
 There’s no indication yet the Alaska effort broke any law, but surely the Trump administration will check.
 This election has been full of gamesmanship.
 Republicans set off a redistricting war to draw themselves more favorable seats in multiple states, starting in Texas. Democrats responded in California, but faltered elsewhere.
 In Montana’s Senate race, many Democrats back an independent, Seth Bodnar, who they feel could win. The Democrat, Alani Bankhead, was backed by a mysterious super PAC that pulled out immediately after she won the primary. She told CNN’s Jake Tapper that Democrats in DC have been conspiring to get her out of the race.
 That race is competitive because Sen. Steve Daines scrapped his reelection campaign on the last possible day, clearing the way for his ally Kurt Alme, who filed to run eight minutes before the deadline.
 Dark money from mysterious sources is meanwhile flooding airwaves with so-called issue ads. There’s a profusion of ads made with AI that put words in candidates’ mouths. Reuters reported that campaigns are investing in efforts to train AI chatbots to control what voters see about them.
 So much in today’s politics is about confusing voters.

 By Fredreka Schouten 
 Service was restored late Wednesday afternoon for an electronic filing system at the federal agency that enforces federal campaign finance laws.
 The Federal Election Commission system had been offline since around 10 p.m. Monday. CNN has not independently verified that information.
 “The electronic filing system is available,” a notice posted on the FEC’s website at 4:50 p.m. Wednesday read. “A fix has been implemented and we are monitoring the results.”
 The outage disrupted the ability of candidates and political committees to file electronic reports detailing last-minute contributions and spending. It came just days before Election Day.
 The agency does not oversee how elections are conducted, and the outage did not affect voting.
